structure.title: 3. Main Identification Results and Estimation Strategies (BLP, GATES, CLAN)
4. Split-Sample Robust Estimation and Inference Methods
5. Further Consideration: Causal Machines That Learn CATE Better

observations.statement: The paper states its estimand as functionals of the CATE (a best linear predictor, sorted group effects, and a classification analysis) rather than the CATE function itself, arguing uniformly valid inference on the full function is generally unattainable without added assumptions.

Identification of the conditional average treatment effect rests on treatment being randomly assigned conditional on covariates, with a propensity score that is known and bounded away from zero and one.
In the empirical application the general conditional-randomization assumption is stated to reduce to simple randomization because the propensity score is constant across units.

The paper frames its contribution as agnostic: it avoids assuming the machine-learning proxy is a consistent estimator of the treatment-effect function, treating it only as a possibly biased and noisy predictor to be post-processed for valid inference.

Sample splitting into an auxiliary sample that trains the machine-learning proxies and a main sample used for post-processing and inference is named as the mechanism that avoids overfitting bias in the reported estimates.

The identification argument is compared explicitly against tree-based and forest-based alternatives from the literature, arguing those approaches require stronger low-dimensionality or sparsity conditions than this paper's agnostic framework.
The empirical sample links administrative monthly vaccination counts from an e-health immunization platform with a separate pre-intervention household baseline survey collected in the same villages.
The analysis panel is structured at the village-by-month level and covers a window equal to the duration of the intervention for the two treatment arms being compared.

The empirical comparison restricts the sample to villages receiving one specific bundled policy versus villages receiving none of the corresponding component treatments, out of a much larger set of cross-randomized combinations in the underlying experiment.
Counts of villages and village-months by treatment status are reported once in the descriptive-statistics table rather than repeated in each subsequent results table.

The outcome is defined as the count of age-eligible children receiving a specific vaccine dose in a village-month, chosen because it is the last dose in the immunization sequence and thus a marker of completed immunization.
Treatment is defined as village-level assignment to a specific combination of nudge interventions rather than to any single component intervention considered in isolation.
The covariate vector used to build machine-learning proxies is a broad set of baseline village-level demographic and prior-immunization variables collected before the intervention began.
Outcomes and covariates are rescaled onto a common bounded range before being passed to the machine-learning training step, applied uniformly across all candidate proxy methods.

The paper states that the village-level regressions used to estimate the key features include district-by-time fixed effects and are weighted by village population, described in implementation-details prose rather than in a table's own notes line.

Result tables report split-aggregated point estimates together with interval bounds in parentheses and two-sided p-values, replacing the coefficient-and-classical-standard-error format common in the applied literature.

Before settling on a main specification, the paper reports a dedicated comparison table ranking several machine-learning proxy methods by goodness-of-fit criteria and carries only the best-performing methods into the main results tables.
Standard errors in the village-level regressions are clustered at the village level, matching the level at which the policy bundle is assigned.
observations.quote: cluster standard errors at the village level

observations.statement: In place of a single asymptotic standard error, confidence intervals and p-values are built by aggregating results across many random splits of the sample, taking medians and quantiles of the split-specific estimates.

When two machine-learning proxy methods are close competitors on the goodness-of-fit criterion, the paper discusses whether to report the union of their confidence sets or apply a discount, and states which convention it adopts and why.

The paper recommends using the un-discounted nominal confidence level rather than a more conservative bound, justifying this by its own numerical evidence that coverage tends to be conservative rather than by a formal guarantee under its weakest assumptions.
A descriptive-statistics table is used to show that treated and control villages have similar baseline characteristics, including prior immunization status, functioning as a covariate balance check.

Goodness-of-fit diagnostics comparing candidate machine-learning proxies are reported with interquartile ranges over repeated splits and used explicitly to decide which methods are carried forward into the main analysis.
The paper reports, in a footnote rather than a table, that results are qualitatively similar under an alternative ratio for dividing the sample into main and auxiliary parts.

Results from purely predictive machine-learning proxies, as opposed to the paper's causal-learner variants, are reported as a robustness comparison placed in a supplemental appendix because they underperform the main causal-learner specification.

The heterogeneity analysis is repeated for an earlier vaccine dose and for a different pair of treatment arms, with the similarity of the qualitative pattern described narratively rather than tabulated, and underlying figures offered only upon request.
An alternative interval-construction rule, aimed at capturing the majority of split-specific values rather than the split-median value, is reported as a robustness check in a supplemental appendix.

Heterogeneity is summarized by sorting units into ranked groups based on a machine-learning-predicted treatment-effect score and comparing the top and bottom groups, rather than by pre-specified covariate subgroups.

The paper frames its group-based heterogeneity approach as a disciplined alternative to the common practice of splitting samples by researcher-chosen covariates after the fact, citing its own review of the literature as evidence such ad hoc analysis is widespread.

Classification analysis is used to describe which baseline characteristics differ between the most- and least-affected groups, with the authors explicitly labeling this association as descriptive rather than causal since it could reflect confounding.
observations.quote: could always be proxying for other things

observations.statement: The pooled average treatment effect implied by the machine-learning-based estimator is compared against the simple raw difference in group means as an informal consistency check on the estimator.

The estimated effect for the most-affected group is benchmarked against effect sizes reported in an earlier published field experiment on immunization incentives to argue the magnitude is plausible rather than implausibly large.

Heterogeneous effects are translated into a cost-effectiveness metric, immunizations delivered per dollar spent, reported separately by heterogeneity group, connecting the statistical results to a policy-relevant monetary interpretation.

The paper reports that estimated heterogeneity-loading coefficients are close to the value indicating a well-calibrated proxy, treating this as an internal precision check on how much the machine-learning score explains the estimated pattern.

The authors state that requiring a pre-specified low-dimensional model of heterogeneity would avoid the power loss induced by sample splitting, framing this loss as the deliberate price for not committing to such a model in advance.

A possible behavioral explanation for the negative effect found in some villages, that nudges crowd out intrinsic motivation, is explicitly presented as one interpretation among others rather than an established finding.
The covariate associations uncovered by the classification analysis are explicitly flagged as potentially reflecting confounding rather than a causal driver of the estimated heterogeneity.

Main result tables report split-aggregated point estimates with interval bounds in parentheses and two-sided p-values in brackets beneath each estimate, a convention explained in each table's own notes rather than through significance stars.
Group-level heterogeneity estimates are displayed in a coefficient-style plot with joint confidence bands alongside a horizontal reference line for the overall average effect.
A descriptive-statistics table reports means of outcome and covariate variables split into overall, treated, and control columns in place of a full distributional summary.
The introduction previews the paper's applied narrative and headline finding of large treatment-effect heterogeneity before the formal theory sections are introduced.

The paper's own roadmap paragraph places the theoretical identification, estimation, and inference sections ahead of the empirical application, with the application and its implementation details positioned only in the section before the conclusion.

The introduction states the paper's three targeted estimands, a best linear predictor, sorted group effects, and a classification analysis, as an explicit list before any formal notation appears, functioning as the contribution paragraph.

Robustness checks for the empirical application are not gathered into a separate labeled robustness subsection but appear as short additional-analysis paragraphs within the results discussion, with much supporting detail deferred to a supplemental appendix.

The authors caution that the estimated heterogeneity pattern is tied to the specific villages and context studied, and recommend piloting similar nudge bundles in new contexts before scaling up rather than assuming automatic generalization.

A public replication package containing code and data is deposited with a persistent DOI, and an editorial note states the journal verified the package's ability to reproduce the paper's reported results.
observations.quote: checked the data and codes ... to reproduce the results

observations.statement: The machine-learning proxy models are implemented through a named R package with specific method identifiers reported for each algorithm used, supporting exact reproduction of the modeling choices.

Outcome data come from an administrative e-health platform that logs immunizations delivered at each program visit, with the paper noting a companion study validated this data against independent field checks.

The underlying experiment had a pre-analysis plan specifying only broad, qualitative categories of covariates for heterogeneity analysis without naming specific variables, a gap the paper presents as motivating its disciplined machine-learning approach.

concordance.paper_says: ML proxies are built with four candidate learners (elastic net, gradient boosting, a neural network, and random forest) via R's caret package, with headline results using a causal-learner (boosting) refinement; post-processing regressions use weighted least squares.
concordance.card_shows: Specifications record random_forest, lasso, and neural_net trained via caret::train, plus weighted-least-squares steps via felm and lm; no specification record corresponds to the gradient-boosting learner or to a causal-learner (boosted) variant.
concordance.note: Card coverage is 'minimal' and its provenance explicitly lists the code files most likely to define the boosting spec and Algorithm 6.2 causal-learner logic as skipped for budget reasons.

concordance.paper_says: The village-level regressions are stated to include district-by-time (month) fixed effects.
concordance.card_shows: A repository-level conventions note records that the code builds a fixed-effect grouping variable from district, year, and month, but the individual specification records leave their own fixed_effects field null.

concordance.paper_says: Standard errors are clustered at the village level.
concordance.card_shows: se.cluster_level is null in every extracted specification (s1, s2, s4, s5, s6, s7); no clustering command was captured from the read portions of the code.

concordance.paper_says: In place of a classical standard-error type, inference is reported as split-aggregated median point estimates with quantile-based interval bounds and median p-values.
concordance.card_shows: se.type is null in every specification, but a separate diagnostics record documents quantile aggregation of p-values and confidence intervals across splits, with an adjustment for the sorted-group comparison.

concordance.paper_says: The main comparison restricts to villages that received one specific bundled policy versus villages that received none of its component treatments, drawn from baseline-survey villages with the intervention implemented.
concordance.card_shows: Two recorded sample restrictions match this: villages flagged as in the baseline survey and first-implementation wave, and villages matching one of two specific combinations of the slope, SMS, gossip, and committee-treatment indicators, plus complete cases on modeling variables.

concordance.paper_says: Village-level estimations are weighted by village population.
concordance.card_shows: A conventions note and the felm/lm specification records show a weight equal to an inverse-propensity-type factor multiplied by an externally supplied population weight.

concordance.paper_says: A dedicated table compares candidate machine-learning proxies on goodness-of-fit criteria across splits and is used to select which methods are carried into the main results.
concordance.card_shows: This comparison is captured only as a table output, not as an entry in the card's diagnostics array, which instead records only the multiple-testing and quantile-aggregation diagnostic.

concordance.paper_says: The treated group receives the full bundled policy (incentives, social-network ambassadors, and reminders); the control group receives none of the sloped-incentive, social-network, or reminder components.
concordance.card_shows: comparison_group is null on every specification record; the underlying grouping is inferable only from raw indicator-variable names in the sample-restriction filter, without a semantic label.

concordance.paper_says: The covariate set used for the proxies and for the classification analysis is a broad list of baseline village-level demographic and prior-immunization variables.
concordance.card_shows: controls_summary is null on every specification and the card's variable_construction array is empty, so no covariate list is recorded in the card.

concordance.paper_says: Robustness checks are reported for an alternative main/auxiliary split ratio, for predictive (non-causal) proxies, for an alternative vaccine outcome and comparison group, and for an alternative interval-aggregation rule.
concordance.card_shows: The card's robustness array is empty, and its provenance explicitly lists the code files most likely to implement these robustness checks as skipped for being out of the reading budget.

concordance.paper_says: The main text presents a descriptive-statistics table, a method-comparison table, tables for the best linear predictor, sorted-group effects, classification analysis, and cost-effectiveness, plus a sorted-group-effects figure; further tables and figures sit in a supplemental appendix.
concordance.card_shows: The card records six table outputs matching the method-comparison, best-linear-predictor, sorted-group, and two appendix-style classification-analysis tables, plus one unresolved figure call, but has no record corresponding to the descriptive-statistics table, the cost-effectiveness table, or the sorted-group figure specifically.
concordance.note: Correspondence holds for the outputs the card does capture; several main-text outputs are simply absent given the card's minimal coverage.

concordance.paper_says: The analysis dataset is a village-by-month panel built from administrative immunization records merged with a baseline household survey.
concordance.card_shows: The card records a single input dataset at village-month level, typed as experimental data, with unknown access and source detail, and no record of the baseline-survey merge.

gaps: No formal balance-test statistic (e.g., a joint test or per-variable significance test) accompanies the descriptive-statistics table; balance is asserted narratively from the reported means alone.

No explicit discussion of attrition or of whether any villages or village-months were dropped after random assignment; the panel is described as approximately balanced but no attrition analysis is reported.
No stated multiple-testing adjustment for the many individual covariates examined in the classification analysis, beyond the adjustment applied to the sorted-group comparison itself.

The paper repeatedly refers to a Supplemental Appendix for proofs and additional tables and figures; that document is not part of the provided text, so diagnostics, robustness, and magnitude details located only there could not be checked directly.

No explicit ex ante power calculation or minimum-detectable-effect statement is given for the heterogeneity analysis in the empirical application itself, though the conclusion discusses sample-size requirements for detecting heterogeneity in general terms.

reading.note: Read the full main text continuously: title/abstract, introduction, the theoretical framework and identification sections (2-5), the empirical application and implementation details (6), and the conclusion (7). The alphabetical reference list (roughly pages 41-43) was read but contains only bibliographic citations with no practice content. The paper's own Supplemental Appendix, cited throughout for proofs and additional tables/figures (Appendices A-H), is a separate document not included among the inputs and was not read.
